title: Study Abroad Report: University of Freiburg
paragraphs: I was allowed to do a three-month clerkship at Freiburg University Hospital. The University of Freiburg is located in southwestern Germany, and its hospital is one of the largest in Germany. Through this program I was able to gain much learning and valuable experience. Below I report on the content of the clerkship in each department and on life there.

Month 1: Thoracic surgery. The clerkship consisted of attending morning rounds and conferences, drawing blood with the local students, and taking part in surgery. In clerkships in Japan the opportunities for blood draws are limited, so I was anxious, but I was taught carefully by the PJs (local sixth-year students called Practical Year, who do practical clerkships), and even when I failed, the patients spoke kind words to me, so I gradually got used to it and became able to draw blood alone with confidence. In surgery, in addition to observing thoracoscopic and robot-assisted surgery, I was allowed into the surgical field as second assistant in open chest surgery. There were days when I felt impatient, thinking I was not receiving enough explanation about the surgery and was learning little, but by asking questions I had anatomy and procedures explained to me, I was allowed to do plate fixation in rib fracture surgery, and I think I was able to have various experiences. Before performing surgery they do a bronchoscopy to confirm the course of the bronchi, and when I was allowed to do it once, I was told, "You're so good it doesn't seem like your first time, you should go into a department that does endoscopy," which made me very happy and left an impression.

Month 2: Obstetrics and gynecology. Many students took part in the clerkship, and the PJs took the lead in managing the students' schedule and dividing up the work. I was included among them and was able to gain a wide range of experience, including observing vaginal deliveries, gynecological surgery, cesarean sections and rounds. In delivery observation, the local midwife was strict with me, who could not speak German, and sometimes did not let me into the delivery room, which was frustrating. But basically they were all warm doctors, who explained a lot in English and gave me opportunities to assist in robotic surgery, laparoscopic surgery, cesarean sections and so on. In particular, when I was given the chance to do breast surgery with just the doctor and me, although he is a doctor who is reputed among students to be educational, I felt I was recognized as one medical student, and I was very happy. Also, on the ward, the pregnant women's partners were always present, and some rooms had a bed set up for the partner. This is a big difference from Japan, and I felt the difference in cultural values about childbirth.

Month 3: Otolaryngology. In otolaryngology I did rounds, observed surgery and observed outpatient clinics. Since I am interested in tumors, I was assigned to the tumor ward and was allowed to observe pre- and postoperative rounds and procedures for oral, pharyngeal and laryngeal cancer. In surgery observation I saw various operations in the head and neck region, and microsurgery and large-scale reconstruction were especially interesting. In the outpatient clinic, many patients came, from children to the elderly, and the process in which, from history taking through ultrasound and hearing tests, the treatment plan is decided on the spot was very educational. Since I would speak to the local residents myself and accompany them, I could observe various styles of outpatient care with a fresh feeling every day.

Although it was thus a very fulfilling clerkship, difficulties with language became a major issue. Conferences and conversations with patients were basically held in German, there were many scenes in which I could not check the content one by one, and there was time I spent without understanding. At German university hospitals a certain level of German ability is required of exchange students as well, and students from other countries who had come through the Erasmus program could also speak German to some extent. Many of the supervising doctors were fluent in English, so there was no obstacle in communication, but in the situation where I alone could not understand German, I sometimes felt isolated and powerless.

I was able to learn about the differences in medicine between Japan and Germany. The cases and patient populations differ greatly from Japan, and I realized that these differences stem from differences in healthcare systems, the situation of the country, and even values about medical care. The breadth of the medical procedures undertaken by each department and doctor was also very impressive. For example, in thoracic surgery they handle everything consistently from bronchoscopy to surgery and chemotherapy, and in otolaryngology too I could see that even large-scale reconstructive surgery is completed entirely within the department. There was also much to learn about the healthcare delivery system, such as running surgery and anesthesia simultaneously in separate rooms to efficiently handle the number of operations per day, the high cost consciousness regarding medical equipment and medical costs, and the short hospital stays. Through these experiences, I strongly felt that understanding the international background and systems of medicine is indispensable for being involved in clinical practice as a doctor in the future and for providing evidence-based practice and conducting clinical research.

Furthermore, interaction with local medical students was also a great stimulus. My impression was that German medical students have abundant knowledge and always deepen their own thinking through practical clerkships as they learn. When I actually asked questions of the PJs, I was impressed that very accurate and logical answers came back. I myself also had opportunities during the clerkship to take part in practical medical procedures, such as blood draws, ultrasound and serving as second assistant in surgery, which was a very valuable experience. I was reminded of the importance of, in order to acquire the ability to function in the field, not simply doing the task but doing it while thinking about its background and intention. In addition, besides the clerkship at the university hospital, local medical students choose hospitals and departments of their own will and experience internships at multiple facilities. This process is closely tied to career formation, and I was greatly stimulated by their attitude of thinking proactively about the future.

This was my first time staying overseas alone for as long as three months. The University of Freiburg does not provide a dormitory, so I secured accommodation on Airbnb, but the host was kind and I had no trouble in daily life. In an environment where Japanese is not understood, I had to do everything myself, such as using public transportation, everyday shopping and the various procedures related to studying abroad, and at first there was much bewilderment and difficulty. However, through repeated failures and trial and error I gained much learning, and there were also many occasions when I was helped by local people, and I think I gradually adapted to the new environment. Freiburg is a student town and so is lively and safe, and with many stylish independent shops and much nature, it was a comfortable city to live in. On holidays I visited various places locally and could come into contact with the culture and history unique to the region.

Taking part in this study abroad program had been my goal since I attended an open campus in high school. Through the actual three-month clerkship I gained many valuable experiences in various clinical departments, and the days were very fulfilling. I am of a cautious character and tend to stay in a stable environment, but in this study abroad I feel I was able to step out of my comfort zone and grow greatly. I express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone concerned who gave me this valuable opportunity.
